During pregnancy and breastfeeding in Botswana, the study published in AIDS (Volume 27, Pages 1911–1920) explores the implications of HIV management and prevention strategies in maternal and child health. 2. Sinha B, Chowdhury R, Sankar MJ, et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on interventions aimed at improving breastfeeding outcomes. This research, published in Acta Paediatrica (Volume 104, Pages 114–134), provides evidence-based insights into effective breastfeeding practices. 3. Thakwalakwa C, Phiri A, Rollins N, et al. (2014) investigated the growth and HIV-free survival of HIV-exposed infants in Malawi. This randomized trial, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (Volume 66, Pages 181–187), evaluated two complementary feeding interventions in the context of maternal antiretroviral therapy. 4. Thistle P, Bolotin S, Lam E, et al. (2011) examined the role of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV in rural Zimbabwe during a socio-economic crisis. The findings were published in Medicine, Conflict and Survival (Volume 27, Pages 165–176). 5. Thomas TK, Masaba R, Borkowf CB, et al. (2011) conducted the Kisumu Breastfeeding Study in Kenya, a clinical trial assessing the efficacy of triple-antiretroviral prophylaxis in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission through breastfeeding. The results were published in PLoS Medicine (Volume 8, Article e1001015). 6. Tonwe-Gold B, Ekouevi DK, Viho I, et al. (2007) evaluated a two-tiered approach to antiretroviral treatment and the prevention of peripartum and postnatal HIV transmission in West Africa. This study was published in PLoS Medicine (Volume 4, Article e257). 7. UNAIDS (2011) outlined a global plan to eliminate new HIV infections among children by 2015 and ensure the survival of their mothers. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 8. UNICEF, UNAIDS, WHO, UNFPA (2003) provided guidelines for decision-makers on HIV and infant feeding. This resource was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 9. Victora CG, Bahl R, Barros AJD, et al. (2016) discussed the epidemiology, mechanisms, and lifelong effects of breastfeeding in the 21st century. This comprehensive review was published in The Lancet (Volume 387, Pages 475–490). 10. Wells GA, Shea B, O’Connell D, et al. (2009) introduced the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for assessing the quality of non-randomized studies in meta-analyses. This methodology was detailed in the book Introduction to Meta-Analysis (West Sussex: Wiley). 11. WHO (2003) developed a global strategy on infant and young child feeding, which was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 12. WHO (2005) published guiding principles for feeding non-breastfed children aged 6–24 months. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 13. WHO (2010a) introduced the Essential Newborn Care Course, which was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 14. WHO (2010b) released guidelines on HIV and infant feeding, providing principles and recommendations for infant feeding in the context of HIV. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 15. WHO (2010c) issued recommendations for the use of antiretroviral drugs in pregnant women to prevent HIV infection in infants. This 2010 revision was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 16. WHO (2012a) updated its framework for priority actions on HIV and infant feeding, which was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 17. WHO (2013) consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, emphasizing a public health approach. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 18. WHO (2014) published a handbook for guideline development, which was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 19. WHO (2015) provided guidance on caring for newborns at home and in the community. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 20. WHO (2016a) described the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) approach, which was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 21. WHO (2016b) provided resources on breastfeeding, which were accessed online on June 13, 2016. 22. WHO (2016c) consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection. This publication was in press at the time. 23. WHO and FAO (2007) issued guidelines on the safe preparation, storage, and handling of powdered infant formula. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 24. WHO and UNICEF (2006) developed an integrated course on infant and young child feeding counseling. This resource was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 25. WHO, UNFPA, UNICEF, and the World Bank (2015) published the third edition of a guide on pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, and newborn care. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 26. WHO, UNICEF, UNAIDS, and UNFPA (2006) provided an update on HIV and infant feeding based on a technical consultation held in Geneva, Switzerland, in October 2006. This document was accessed online on June 13, 2016. 27. Zunza M, Mercer GD, Thabane L, et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review on the effects of postnatal interventions for reducing vertical HIV transmission on infant growth and non-HIV infections. This study was published in Journal of the International AIDS Society (Volume 16, Article 18865). 28. Chikhungu L, Bispo S, Newell ML. conducted systematic reviews on HIV-free survival and postnatal HIV transmission rates in breastfed infants of HIV-positive mothers on ART. These reviews were commissioned for guideline development and accessed online in 2016. 29. Mallampati D, MacLean R, Ciaranello A. modeled the impact of maternal antiretroviral use and infant mortality. This study was commissioned for guideline development and accessed online in 2016. 30. The WHO Guideline Development Group examined the implications of updated recommendations on infant feeding guidance for mothers living with HIV, particularly in conflict or emergency settings, and the implications for monitoring and evaluation.
